analysis.one_liner: Makes community college tuition-free nationwide through federal-state grants.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a vote: referred to the Senate education committee in October 2023 with 10 Democratic cosponsors, it died there when the Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have made public community college tuition-free by having the federal government pay states to waive tuition and fees for eligible students, with states covering a share that grows from 0% to 20% over five years. It also created a $1 billion-a-year fund to help colleges improve graduation and transfer rates, and gave grants to historically Black colleges, tribal colleges, and minority-serving institutions to waive the first 60 credits for low-income students. It was referred to the Senate education committee in October 2023 and never received a vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Students at public community colleges would pay $0 in tuition and fees as long as they attend at least half time, within a six-semester limit. Low-income students at historically Black colleges, tribal colleges, and minority-serving institutions would get their first 60 credits waived or sharply reduced. States, tribal colleges, and community colleges themselves gain a new federal funding stream, and community college students gain guaranteed transfer of associate degrees into four-year public universities. Eligibility cannot be denied based on immigration status.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Community college students, especially low-income ones

how_it_helps.text: Sets tuition and fees at $0 for eligible community college students enrolled at least half time, for up to six semesters of free attendance.
Pays the federal share through grants to states and tribal colleges, starting at 100% of average community college tuition and phasing down to 80%, with states picking up the rest.
Gives grants to historically Black colleges, tribal colleges, and minority-serving institutions to waive or sharply reduce tuition for the first 60 credits for low-income students.
Creates a $1 billion-a-year Student Success Fund for mentoring, advising, childcare, transportation, and other supports aimed at low-income, first-generation, and underserved students.
Requires participating states to make associate degrees fully transferable to public four-year universities and to align high school graduation with college-ready coursework.
Bars participating states from imposing extra eligibility requirements and prohibits denying benefits based on immigration status.

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers would fund the program under an open-ended appropriation ("such sums as may be necessary" for every fiscal year), plus a permanent $1 billion annual Student Success Fund and roughly $2.5 billion a year for college grants by 2033. States that opt in would pay a rising share of tuition costs, from 0% the first year to 20% by 2028-29, and must keep their own higher education spending from falling below three-year averages.
analysis.who_pays_short: Federal taxpayers; states pay a rising match

drawbacks.text: The federal share is an open-ended appropriation ('such sums as may be necessary') on top of a permanent $1 billion annual Student Success Fund and roughly $2.5 billion a year for college grants by 2033, making it a large permanent claim on the budget with no revenue offset in the bill.

States would owe a rising share of costs, reaching 20% by 2028-29, and must not reduce their own higher education funding below three-year averages, which some states could see as an unfunded federal mandate.
The benefit is limited: it covers tuition and fees only, not living costs, and community college students lose eligibility after six semesters of free attendance.

Critics of free-tuition proposals generally argue that subsidizing all community college students, including those who could afford to pay, costs more per added student than targeted aid; the bill would apply the benefit regardless of income.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is concrete and large for the people it reaches: two years of free community college, better transfer guarantees, and extra support for underserved students, aimed mostly at low- and middle-income families. The cost is also real: an open-ended federal commitment plus permanent annual appropriations, with states on the hook for a fifth of costs and a maintenance-of-effort floor. Whether free tuition for all income levels is the most cost-effective way to expand access is a fair objection, but the bill's design includes state matching funds, evidence-based reforms, and outcome reporting to blunt the worst quality concerns. The decisive fact is that none of this weighing happened in Congress: the bill never got a vote, so neither its benefits nor its costs were ever tested.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate education committee and sat there until the Congress ended, never reaching a vote.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on October 19, 2023, with 10 Democratic cosponsors signing on the same day.
It was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions, which took no further action on it.
The Congress ended on January 3, 2025, with no committee markup, no floor vote, and no House action on a companion measure.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Students gained nothing, since no free-tuition program was created. For-profit colleges and other institutions that rely on tuition and loan-financed enrollment kept the status quo, and taxpayers were spared a permanent new open-ended federal spending commitment.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Colleges and lenders that collect tuition and loan interest

for.name: Sen. Tammy Baldwin
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited 10 Democratic cosponsors on the day of introduction.

for.name: 10 of 48 Senate Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; no Republican signed on.

against.name: Senate HELP Committee
against.role: Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral in October 2023 and took no further action on it for the rest of the Congress; no markup, no hearing action, no committee vote appears in the record.

against.name: Sen. Chuck Schumer
against.what_they_did: Did not bring the bill to the Senate floor or act on it in any way before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: No vote ever occurred; the only visible support was 11 Democratic senators with no Republican cosponsor, so partisan shape can only be inferred from sponsorship.

industries.note: The bill would have routed a large new federal funding stream to public two-year colleges and made enrollment free for students, boosting access and resources.
A free public community college option competes directly with for-profit schools for tuition-paying students. The bill's demise preserves their enrollment and revenue.

industries.industry: HBCUs, tribal colleges, and minority-serving institutions
industries.note: They would have received dedicated grants to waive or cut the first 60 credits of tuition for low-income students, a direct revenue and enrollment benefit.
Maintenance-of-effort rules would have barred states from cutting operating support, and transfer-pathway requirements would have steered more students into public four-year programs.
Free tuition for the first two years reduces the amount students must borrow for community college. The bill's failure leaves borrowing needs unchanged.
